marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q001.takeaway: Lung capillaries are continuous; fenestrated capillaries occur in organs with high exchange needs such as kidney, endocrine glands and intestine.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q001.displayText:
Lung capillaries are continuous; fenestrated capillaries occur in organs with high exchange needs such as kidney, endocrine glands and intestine.

Fenestrated capillaries are absent in the lungs.

Fenestrated capillaries contain gaps between endothelial cells and occur where passage of larger molecules is required, including renal glomeruli, endocrine glands, intestinal mucosa and pancreas.
emphasis: Lung capillaries are continuous; fenestrated capillaries occur in organs with high exchange needs such as kidney, endocrine glands and intestine

rationales.a: Renal glomeruli contain fenestrated capillaries for filtration.
rationales.c: Endocrine glands use fenestrated capillaries to facilitate hormone exchange.
rationales.d: Small-intestinal villi have fenestrated capillaries that aid absorption.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q002.takeaway: Vasa vasorum nourish the outer tunica media and adventitia of large vessel walls, where diffusion from the lumen is inadequate.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q002.displayText:
Vasa vasorum nourish the outer tunica media and adventitia of large vessel walls, where diffusion from the lumen is inadequate.

Vasa vasorum is a network of small vessels supplying the tunica adventitia and outer tunica media of large vessels.

Small arteries are nourished by diffusion from luminal blood; in larger arteries diffusion becomes inadequate, so vasa vasorum supply the adventitia and outer media while the intima and inner media are nourished from the lumen.
emphasis: Vasa vasorum nourish the outer tunica media and adventitia of large vessel walls, where diffusion from the lumen is inadequate

rationales.a: Vasa vasorum also supply the outer tunica media, so adventitia alone is too limited.
rationales.c: The inner media and intima are mainly nourished by luminal diffusion; vasa vasorum do not supply all of media.
rationales.d: Vasa vasorum do not extend to the inner tunica intima.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q003.takeaway: Collateral circulation is blood flow through arterial or venous anastomoses that link alternate pathways.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q003.displayText:
Collateral circulation is blood flow through arterial or venous anastomoses that link alternate pathways.

Circulation through anastomoses is called collateral circulation.

Anastomoses may be arterial, venous or arteriovenous. Examples include palmar/plantar arches and Circle of Willis for arterial anastomoses, dorsal venous arches for venous anastomoses, and AV shunts in skin, lips, ears, nasal/intestinal mucosa and erectile tissue.
emphasis: Collateral circulation is blood flow through arterial or venous anastomoses that link alternate pathways

rationales.a: Capillaries are exchange vessels, not the named connecting pathway that defines collateral circulation.
rationales.b: Sinusoids are specialized vascular spaces, not connecting collateral channels.
rationales.d: Plexus describes a network, but the specific term for alternate communicating channels is anastomosis.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q004.takeaway: Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated fetal blood from the fetus to the placenta, an exception to the usual oxygenation pattern.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q004.displayText:
Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated fetal blood from the fetus to the placenta, an exception to the usual oxygenation pattern.

Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the heart to the placenta during fetal life.

Arteries generally carry oxygenated blood away from the heart; pulmonary and umbilical arteries are exceptions carrying deoxygenated blood.
emphasis: Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated fetal blood from the fetus to the placenta, an exception to the usual oxygenation pattern

rationales.a: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; pulmonary and umbilical arteries show oxygenation exceptions.
rationales.b: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
rationales.c: Arteries generally lack valves along their course; semilunar valves are at the ventricular outlets.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q005.takeaway: Muscular arterioles provide the major adjustable resistance to blood flow and strongly influence peripheral vascular resistance.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q005.displayText:
Muscular arterioles provide the major adjustable resistance to blood flow and strongly influence peripheral vascular resistance.

Muscular arterioles contribute the major part of peripheral resistance to blood flow.

Arterioles are the smallest muscular arteries and have relatively thick tunica media. They produce the largest pressure drop before capillary beds, are densely sympathetically innervated, and are regulated mainly by local vasoactive/metabolic factors with central mechanisms also contributing.
emphasis: Muscular arterioles provide the major adjustable resistance to blood flow and strongly influence peripheral vascular resistance

rationales.a: Elastic arteries dampen pulsatile flow but are not the principal resistance vessels.
rationales.b: Small muscular arteries contribute resistance, but arterioles are the dominant resistance-control site.
rationales.c: Capillaries are exchange vessels; their combined cross-sectional area keeps flow slow.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q007.takeaway: Testicular veins normally contain valves; several large visceral and cerebral veins listed lack valves.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q007.displayText:
Testicular veins normally contain valves; several large visceral and cerebral veins listed lack valves.

Testicular veins have valves.

Venous valves maintain unidirectional blood flow. The source lists valve absence in veins less than 2 mm, venae cavae, and hepatic, renal, uterine, ovarian, cerebral, spinal, pulmonary and umbilical veins; it also notes the fetal Eustachian valve of the IVC.
emphasis: Testicular veins normally contain valves; several large visceral and cerebral veins listed lack valves

rationales.b: The inferior vena cava lacks valves along most of its course.
rationales.c: Cerebral veins and dural venous sinuses are generally valveless.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q008.takeaway: Parotid glands contain ordinary continuous capillaries; sinusoids are found in organs such as liver, spleen and endocrine tissues.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q008.displayText:
Parotid glands contain ordinary continuous capillaries; sinusoids are found in organs such as liver, spleen and endocrine tissues.

Sinusoids are absent in parotid glands.

Sinusoids are large irregular vascular spaces with true discontinuities in their walls, allowing close contact between blood and organ parenchyma. The source lists liver, spleen, bone marrow, suprarenal glands, adenohypophysis, parathyroid glands and carotid body as sites containing sinusoids.
emphasis: Parotid glands contain ordinary continuous capillaries; sinusoids are found in organs such as liver, spleen and endocrine tissues

rationales.a: Suprarenal glands have sinusoidal capillaries, facilitating endocrine exchange.
rationales.b: Parathyroid tissue is endocrine and has fenestrated/sinusoidal capillary beds.
rationales.d: The carotid body has a rich sinusoidal capillary network for chemoreceptor exchange.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q009.takeaway: Veins have less elastic tissue than corresponding arteries, along with thinner walls and usually larger lumens.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q009.displayText:
Veins have less elastic tissue than corresponding arteries, along with thinner walls and usually larger lumens.

Compared with corresponding arteries, veins have much less muscular and elastic tissue, consistent with lower venous pressure.
emphasis: Veins have less elastic tissue than corresponding arteries, along with thinner walls and usually larger lumens

rationales.a: Veins generally have a larger lumen than paired arteries, so this is a true difference.
rationales.b: Valves are present in many veins and absent in most corresponding arteries.
rationales.c: Venous walls are thinner than those of corresponding arteries.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q011.takeaway: Lymph nodes receive afferent lymphatic vessels and send efferent vessels from the hilum.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q011.displayText:
Lymph nodes receive afferent lymphatic vessels and send efferent vessels from the hilum.

Lymph nodes have both afferent and efferent lymphatics. Afferent lymphatics enter at multiple points on the periphery and efferent lymphatics leave at the hilum.

The source notes that tonsils, thymus and spleen have no afferent lymphatics.
emphasis: Lymph nodes receive afferent lymphatic vessels and send efferent vessels from the hilum

rationales.a: The spleen filters blood and has no afferent lymphatic vessels.
rationales.b: The thymus receives lymphatic drainage but does not have afferent lymphatics.
rationales.d: Tonsils have efferent lymphatics but lack afferent lymphatics.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q012.takeaway: The right upper limb drains to the right lymphatic duct; the thoracic duct drains the left upper limb and both lower limbs.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q012.displayText:
The right upper limb drains to the right lymphatic duct; the thoracic duct drains the left upper limb and both lower limbs.

The right upper limb drains into the right lymphatic duct rather than the thoracic duct.

The thoracic duct drains both lower limbs, left upper limb, abdomen, left half of thorax and left side of head/neck. The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper limb, right half of thorax and right side of head/neck.
emphasis: The right upper limb drains to the right lymphatic duct; the thoracic duct drains the left upper limb and both lower limbs

rationales.b: The right lower limb drains to the thoracic duct.
rationales.c: The left upper limb drains to the thoracic duct, not the right lymphatic duct.
rationales.d: The left lower limb drains to the thoracic duct.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q013.takeaway: Lymphatic capillaries are wider and more permeable than blood capillaries; they begin as blind-ended vessels in tissues.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q013.displayText:
Lymphatic capillaries are wider and more permeable than blood capillaries; they begin as blind-ended vessels in tissues.

Lymph capillaries are wider than blood capillaries, so the statement that they are narrower is false.

They begin blindly in tissue spaces, form networks, have thin permeable endothelial walls and relatively lower pressure than blood capillaries.
emphasis: Lymphatic capillaries are wider and more permeable than blood capillaries; they begin as blind-ended vessels in tissues

rationales.a: Lymphatic capillaries do begin blindly in interstitial spaces.
rationales.c: Their endothelial wall is thin and highly permeable to fluid and macromolecules.
rationales.d: Lymph flow is low-pressure compared with blood capillary flow.

marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q014.takeaway: There are eight pairs of cervical spinal nerves: C1–C7 exit above their vertebrae and C8 exits below C7.
marrow__ANAT_CH62_Q014.displayText:
There are eight pairs of cervical spinal nerves: C1–C7 exit above their vertebrae and C8 exits below C7.

There are 8 pairs of cervical spinal nerves.

The cerebrospinal nervous system includes 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal.
emphasis: There are eight pairs of cervical spinal nerves: C1–C7 exit above their vertebrae and C8 exits below C7

rationales.a: Six pairs omits the C7 and C8 nerves.
rationales.b: Seven cervical vertebrae do not mean seven spinal nerve pairs; there are eight.
rationales.d: Nine pairs exceeds the standard eight cervical spinal nerve pairs.
